stories.topic: The Planner and the Doer (Personal Separation of Powers)
stories.summary: Ajay describes a personal productivity framework where he splits himself into two distinct selves: the Planner and the Doer. The Planner sits down and lays out everything that needs to be done — priorities, probabilities, calendar slots. Then the Doer takes over and executes mindlessly, refusing to plan or second-guess. When the Doer is at the desk, the Planner is gone; you trust your earlier judgment, blow off all other deadlines, and 'be there fully' on the one thing.
stories.insight: A productivity hack with deep philosophical roots — the same separation-of-powers logic applied to the self. Mixing planning and doing is how anxiety wins; separating them is how you get the 'full pleasure of doing one thing at a time well.' Trust the prior version of yourself who chose.

stories.topic: The Three Amits — Planner, Doer, Regretter
stories.summary: Amit's self-deprecating extension of Ajay's frame: within him there is Amit the Planner ('he can plan everything perfectly, man'), Amit the Doer ('a freaking nikama'), and a third — Amit the Regretter — who, like Brando in On the Waterfront, mourns 'I could have been a contender.' The Regretter is what shows up when Doer fails Planner.
stories.insight: A useful taxonomy of failure modes for any framework of self-discipline. The Doer is supposed to liberate the Planner by absorbing all the executional risk — but if he doesn't show up, the Regretter takes over and turns lost work into self-recrimination.

stories.topic: The Magna Carta — A Knife to King John's Throat
stories.summary: In 1215, a bunch of merchants and finance people physically caught King John, put a knife to his throat, and forced him to sign a document — what we now call the Magna Carta. The text reads as fossilised and archaic today, but it was the world's first clear enunciation that the king is not absolute, that royal authority has limits.
stories.insight: The constraints on power that we treat as abstract principles were, at their origin, extracted by physical force from someone who didn't want to give them up. Liberty wasn't conferred — it was wrested. A reminder that the 'paper' of constitutionalism rests on much older, much more violent acts of insistence.

stories.topic: Nehru, Lal Bahadur Shastri, and the Babri Idol
stories.summary: When the Ram idol was planted in the Babri Masjid, Jawaharlal Nehru in Delhi immediately ordered its removal — within a couple of days, before things spiralled. But the chief minister of UP was Govind Ballabh Pant and the deputy chief minister was Lal Bahadur Shastri, who would have had to carry out the order. Shastri refused. Both men were Congress, but the central diktat could be ignored — until the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi centralised the party and chief ministers became appointees of the high command.
stories.insight: The Congress of the 50s and 60s had genuine internal democracy and federalism — local politicians could defy the centre. The decay of intra-party democracy under Indira Gandhi is the lesser-told twin of the Anti-Defection Bill: together they hollowed out the legislature and made the executive supreme. Amit notes wryly that on this particular instance he wishes Shastri had obeyed — but the principle of local autonomy was healthier than what replaced it.

stories.topic: Standing Committees — A Norm That Powered the 1991-2011 Boom
stories.summary: From Shivraj Patil onwards, India developed an informal norm for standing committees. A bill would be tabled; if there was meaningful opposition, the speaker would refer it to a standing committee chaired by an opposition MP. The committee — ruling and opposition together — would open up the bill, debate it, summon expert witnesses, interrogate the civil servants who drafted it. Ajay served as an expert before many. It was 'fabulous'... but it lived only in norms, not in rules. Today it has effectively vanished.
stories.insight: Public choice theory's hardest lesson: norms decay, only rules endure. Some of India's best institutional innovations (standing committees, intra-party democracy) were never codified — and so they were 'whisked away in no time.' If you want a check to survive, write it into the constitution.

stories.topic: SEBI — The Investigator, Prosecutor, and Judge Have Lunch Together
stories.summary: In SEBI's original design, the same body drafts the regulation, conducts the investigation, decides to prosecute, AND adjudicates. A SEBI employee plays judge while his colleague is the prosecutor; appeals went to a board member of SEBI itself. Early SEBI orders read 'I hereby find Amit Varma guilty of horrible crimes and impose a fine of 10 crore rupees' — with no explanation, no logical argument. Contrast with the SEC, where the courtroom physically sits inside the SEC building but the administrative law judge is a member of the U.S. judiciary, not an SEC employee.
stories.insight: A vivid case study of what 'no separation of powers' actually looks like in a regulator. The investigator, prosecutor, and judge eating lunch together is not a metaphor — it is a structural fact. India is '30% into' fixing this; the rest is TBD.

stories.topic: The Striking Down of Chevron Deference (2024)
stories.summary: Chevron deference, a U.S. doctrine since the 1980s, said that when an agency expert had applied her mind and drafted a regulation, judges could not reopen it on substance — only on process. In 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court largely struck Chevron down, ruling that even if a civil servant has 15 PhDs and is the world's leading expert, a judge can still reopen the substantive content of a regulation. Around the same time, the Court struck down the SEC's in-house administrative-law-judge arrangement as unconstitutional, on the grounds that the defendant had a right to a jury trial.
stories.insight: Two huge 2024 developments rolling back the U.S. administrative state — and a reminder that the line between 'expert agency' and 'unaccountable lawmaker' is genuinely contested in mature democracies. The pendulum can swing back; institutional design is never settled.

stories.topic: Tarunabh Khaitan on the Real Check on Judges
stories.summary: Ajay relays the legal scholar Tarunabh Khaitan's argument: you cannot — and should not — get a check and balance against a judge from the legislature or executive. So what disciplines a bad judge? The answer is peers, lawyers, and academics. A judge who writes a poor ruling loses standing among other judges, sees lawyers ridicule her in chambers, and finds law bloggers and academic journals dissecting the order. The currency is professional respect.
stories.insight: Norms still matter even after the formal separation of powers is built. The judiciary self-regulates through reputation — which means the health of legal academia, law blogs, and bar associations is a load-bearing input into the rule of law itself.

stories.topic: Angela Merkel on the Soul of Germany
stories.summary: Ajay recalls Merkel saying that we will know the true soul of Germany only when the last people who lived through the Second World War have died — only then will we see what today's young Germans have actually internalised. The recent German elections, with about 20% voting for AfD, suggest the lessons of the 20th century are not automatically transmitted.
stories.insight: Every generation has to fight its own battles for liberty — institutions don't run on inertia. Just because your parents built a great country doesn't mean you inherit one; it means you inherit a job.

recommendations.creator: David Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's libertarian classic on the institutional architecture that produces freedom.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes the title as the perfect phrase for the work of going from abstract principles (dispersion of power, checks and balances) to living, breathing institutions — decentralisation, separation of powers, the split between investigator and prosecutor. Amit's heart 'filled with freaking joy and bloom' because he didn't expect this libertarian reference from 'the secret statist.'

recommendations.creator: Manam Chocolate (Hyderabad)
recommendations.context: A Hyderabad company making expensive, genuinely high-quality chocolate.
recommendations.reason: Pure indulgence pick. Ajay clarifies it is unsponsored — 'Manam chocolate is awesome.'

recommendations.creator: Andrew E. Dessler
recommendations.context: Dessler's 2022 third edition — a slim, sensible 200-page primer covering climate science, mitigation, and adaptation.
recommendations.reason: Climate change is 'one of the great crises of the modern world right up there alongside populism' and you'll get the gist from this single book. Sensibly written, accessible to non-specialists.

recommendations.creator: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
recommendations.context: The flagship reports of the IPCC.
recommendations.reason: Ajay is 'normally very skeptical' about international-body reports (World Bank, IMF — bland, written by committee), but the IPCC's are awesome. Written by committees of scientists with proper processes for discussion and debate, they show state-of-the-art thinking AND portray the disagreements (clutch of models, range of scenarios). 'Just look at all the pictures' — the graphics will change the way you look at the world.

recommendations.creator: Ian Kershaw
recommendations.context: Kershaw's 2007 history of the ten decisions that shaped 1940-41.
recommendations.reason: Especially timely amid the collapse of the Atlantic Alliance. Centres on how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side — until August 1941 about half the House of Representatives still didn't want to do it. Gives insights into America and into the present moment.

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: A song from Led Zeppelin's Physical Graffiti.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pick for 'the greatest Led Zep song that is not widely known.' Worth really sitting with if you haven't already.

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.reason: Ajay challenges listeners to first read the lyrics on the page and ask what kind of song you would make from those lines — because that is what happened to him many years ago, and the actual song is surprising and brilliant. 'It'll just make you think about songs.'

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: From In Through the Out Door, the last Zeppelin album before John Bonham's death and the band's break-up.
recommendations.reason: Ajay considers it 'one of the great things' Robert Plant, Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones, and Bonzo did. They were at the peak of their powers — and a poignant pick because Bonham died shortly after.

recommendations.item: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The earlier EIE episode on dispersing power vertically — between union, state, and city.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode to this one. Decentralisation and separation of powers are the two grand mechanisms of dispersing power; this episode handles the second, that one the first.

recommendations.item: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Episode 88, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The recent EIE episode on free speech.
recommendations.reason: Referenced for the discussion of Nehru's First Amendment as a contextualised mistake — and for the larger point that the Indian constitution 'doesn't protect free speech at all.'

recommendations.item: The Anti-Defection Law (Episode 13, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
recommendations.context: An early TSATU episode on the Anti-Defection Law.
recommendations.reason: Explains how the well-intentioned Anti-Defection Bill of the late 1980s ended all genuine debate in Parliament — you can now 'run Parliament from an Excel sheet.' Foundational for understanding why India's legislature has atrophied.

recommendations.item: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with M. R. Madhavan
recommendations.context: A long TSATU episode with M. R. Madhavan on the workings of the Indian Parliament.
recommendations.reason: Both Amit and Ajay admire Madhavan; he goes deep on the Anti-Defection Bill and the death of legislative independence. Essential companion listening.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the place where Ajay tells the inspiring story of SEBI's founding — Surendra Dave, Ravi Narain, and the others who imagined and drafted the SEBI Act.

recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: An annual conference where Ajay and his XKDR colleagues convene scholars and practitioners.
recommendations.reason: Last year's conference had an entire session on recent developments in the U.S. administrative state — 'a field that is red hot with interesting developments and beautiful, interesting intellectual debates.'

recommendations.creator: U.S. Congress
recommendations.context: A slim 1946 U.S. law that is the single rule book for ALL federal agencies — not separate rules for the SEC vs. Fed vs. EPA.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'a phenomenal piece of work... a blueprint for the checks and balances that should reside in federal agencies.' One law for every agency, because the basic principles of hygiene, transparency, and checks and balances do not vary by sector. India's draft Indian Financial Code (140 sections, one rule book for all financial agencies) was inspired by it.

recommendations.item: How Substantial Are Non-Substantive Hearings? (XKDR paper on Indian courts)
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: An XKDR paper providing quantitative evidence on Bombay High Court and Delhi High Court performance.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's defence against the old assumption (held by Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain in the 1990s) that the Bombay High Court is 'absolutely horrible, nothing will ever get done.' The paper shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and improving — meaning the case for keeping a quasi-judicial function inside SEBI has weakened.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Plugged in the description as the hosts' newly launched offering.

core_ideas.concept: Democracy Is Dispersion of Power, Not Just Voting
core_ideas.explanation: Many people behave as if democracy is all about voting — picking a candidate who then 'rules over them.' But that would be a sad world, because then you've just used voting to choose a king, and the king becomes impossible to unseat. The essence of democracy is checks and balances and dispersion of power. Voting is merely the way you select who plays a legislative role. Decentralisation (vertical dispersion: union/state/city) and separation of powers (horizontal dispersion: legislature/executive/judiciary) are the two grand mechanisms.
core_ideas.quote: It would be a very sad world in which voting was used to choose a king.

core_ideas.concept: Separation of Powers — The Three Co-Equal Branches
core_ideas.explanation: Cut the state vertically into three pieces, give each its own lane, and never let one override another. The legislature writes laws (only legislators can write a law — to do so you must win an election). The executive (police, prosecutor) implements: takes complaints, investigates against the written text, but cannot decide what is a crime nor who deserves punishment. The judiciary (and only the judiciary) decides whether punishment applies, after hearing both sides. This is 'a mind-blowing achievement in political philosophy' — Montesquieu's synthesis, drawing on earlier thinkers, made constitutionally explicit for the first time in Articles 1, 2, 3 of the U.S. Constitution.
core_ideas.quote: This is not a happy family, this is not a harmonious family, it's a game of conflict.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's personal-productivity application of the same principle: split yourself into a planning self and an executing self, and never let them overlap. The Planner does all the cognitive work — priorities, probabilities, scheduling. Then the Doer takes the field, refuses to plan or revise, trusts the Planner's judgment, and executes mindlessly. 'When you are there, be there fully... we get the full pleasure of doing one thing at a time well.' Then Mr. Doer is kicked out and the Planner returns to choose what to do next.
core_ideas.quote: The doer will not think or plan. The doer will just implement mindlessly.

core_ideas.explanation: An American phrase Ajay urges all to adopt: 'a world where officials of the executive branch disproportionately exert legislative and judicial powers.' Began globally with FDR's 1930s expansion. India is the worst-case version — joint secretaries write laws, district collectors call themselves district magistrates and play judge, civil servants draft regulations and adjudicate them. Even the U.S. Republicans 'cannot even imagine an administrative state of this nature.' India's case has multiple causes: the original Constitution's silence on separation of powers, the Anti-Defection Bill, and the 1970s centralisation of party power.
core_ideas.quote: The administrative state is a world where officials of the executive branch disproportionately exert legislative and judicial powers.

core_ideas.explanation: A specific legal flaw: when Parliament gives unelected officials a lawmaking function, that delegation must be narrow and tightly controlled. The original SEBI Act had 'excessive delegation' — vast unchecked rule-making power handed to civil servants. The squeamishness this should produce is the right instinct: regulations are laws, and 'unelected officials drafting law' is in tension with democratic legitimacy. The fix is not to abolish delegation but to constrain it carefully.

core_ideas.concept: The Basic Structure Doctrine — A Living Constitution
core_ideas.explanation: Indian Supreme Court jurisprudence created an amendment-proof core of the Constitution. It has evolved in three directions: (1) limiting how Parliament can amend the Constitution; (2) becoming a test applied to ALL new legislation, not just amendments; (3) being progressively expanded — Articles 14, 19, the right to life, and now separation of powers itself have been read into it. So although the original Indian Constitution has no meaningful separation of powers, it 'lurks inside the living constitution' today via the basic structure. If you fed the text to an LLM it would say no separation exists; you have to read the jurisprudence.
core_ideas.quote: If you will feed the constitution of India to an LLM, he will say there is no separation of powers here. But you have to read the history correctly.

core_ideas.explanation: James Buchanan's lesson: lines in the constitution and law matter — there must be black-and-white prohibitions that reshape incentives. But that's not enough. Norms — both mass culture and elite culture — also discipline behaviour. A judge who writes a bad ruling loses social standing in the eyes of peers, lawyers, law bloggers, and academic journals. Rules anchor the system; norms keep it healthy day to day. The standing-committees story is the cautionary tale: a great institution that lived only in norms vanished within a generation.

core_ideas.concept: Friction Is a Feature, Not a Bug
core_ideas.explanation: We typically think of friction as bad. But when it comes to the state, friction is the point. A separation-of-powers system is supposed to be slow, contentious, and conflict-laden. The process is the guarantee that nothing hasty is done. Even if a single party captures all three branches over time, having the formal architecture means an authoritarian move is visible to citizens — Indira Gandhi's emergency was a 'visible imposition,' not a quiet pretence of business as usual.
core_ideas.quote: Friction is a check and balance you need.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's worry: any well-designed system, given enough time, tends to decay. A party in power long enough can fill judicial appointments, regulatory boards, and bureaucratic positions with loyalists. Is the atrophy inevitable? Probably yes, by the law of large numbers. But that doesn't argue against separation of powers — it argues that 'eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.' The question is whether the formal architecture survives long enough to make authoritarian capture visible and contestable.

Andrew Breitbart's line, repurposed by Amit. The intellectual conception of liberty is necessary but insufficient — the constitution can spell out separation of powers, but if those values are not anchored in the culture, atrophy will overwhelm them. The task of governance ends not when you draft a constitution but when 'every citizen instinctively says, no, this is a bad thing' whenever freedom is infringed. Today in India, that instinct is missing; people 'look to a strongman.' The deepest battle is cultural, not legal.
core_ideas.quote: Politics is downstream of culture. — Andrew Breitbart

core_ideas.concept: The Anti-Defection Bill — Good Intent, Bad Outcome
core_ideas.explanation: Late-1980s law that locked all MPs of a party into voting whatever the whip says, intended to stop horse-trading and floor-defections. Outcome: ended all parliamentary debate. MPs became extras; bills could be passed from an Excel sheet by the leadership; no MP needed to read or have a view. Combined with the 1970s centralisation of intra-party power (Indira Gandhi appointing chief ministers from the centre, ending the Congress's federated culture), it produced an executive-dominant state. Classic economics lesson — 'don't look at intention, look at outcome.'

Each generation must learn the lessons of liberty for itself; institutions don't transmit values automatically. Angela Merkel: we will know the soul of Germany only when the last people who lived through the Second World War have died. Twenty percent of Germans now vote AfD. The implication for India: just because the Constituent Assembly included extraordinary minds doesn't mean their thinking is now the default cognitive style of citizens. 'Every generation has to figure this out.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's third Amit: alongside Amit the Planner and Amit the Doer there is 'Amit the Regretter' — channelling Brando in On the Waterfront: 'I could have been a contender.'

Ajay on royal absolutism: 'There was monarchy and the power of Emperor Aurangzeb. If Aurangzeb said off with his head, then Mr. Beer Biceps would have no choice. So that would be the end of poor beer biceps.'

Ajay on the economist's monolithic-state assumption: 'You don't have some Aurangzeb and you're supposed to go whisper in Aurangzeb's ears that dude, we should do inflation targeting.' Amit then promises a cartoon of Ajay whispering inflation-targeting advice into Aurangzeb's ear.

Amit on Ajay's libertarian reveal: 'My heart filled with freaking joy and bloom unexpectedly when Ajay mentioned The Machinery of Freedom. I almost feel like I finally, finally found a kindred soul — and guess where? Right here.' Ajay's deadpan reply: 'There is no gulf between the heart and the head — my heart sees the machinery of freedom, but my head has worked out all the compromises.'
Ajay on the SEBI quasi-court: 'The judge and the prosecutor and the investigator go have lunch together and they conduct a little trial.'

Ajay on running Parliament under the Anti-Defection Bill: 'You can run Parliament from an Excel sheet. You don't even need people to show up. Frankly, you don't even need to elect individual legislators.'

Ajay teasing the LLMs: feeding the Indian Constitution to an LLM and asking about separation of powers — 'he will say chai there is no separation of powers here.' You actually have to read the basic-structure jurisprudence.
Ajay on the Dessler climate book: 'Nomsita will stay up at night with edge-of-the-seat excitement around the Dressler book.'

Amit's closing tease — that Ajay's pitch for IPCC reports ('a clutch of models... look at all the pictures... it will change the way you look at the world') applies equally well to a teenager discovering the Sports Illustrated swimsuit edition. 'But you were a different kind of teenager.'
Magna Carta (1215) — invoked as the Ur-document of constraints on power. Merchants and finance people put a knife to King John's throat to force him to sign.
Montesquieu — 17th-18th century French philosopher who synthesised earlier thinking into the explicit doctrine of separation of powers, foundational to the U.S. Constitution.
Max Weber's definition of the state — 'a community that creates and maintains a monopoly of violence.'
James Buchanan and public-choice theory — invoked twice: that intentions don't matter, incentives do; and that norms decay where rules persist.

Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly: explicitly defended NOT importing the American executive-legislature separation, arguing that members of Parliament needed direct guidance and initiative from executive members sitting in Parliament.
Jefferson (alleged): 'Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty' — Amit's invocation against atrophy.
Andrew Breitbart: 'Politics is downstream of culture' — used to argue that the deepest battle for liberty is cultural, not legal.
Angela Merkel: that we will know the true soul of Germany only when the last people who lived through the Second World War have died.
Tarunabh Khaitan — UK-based Indian legal scholar invoked for the argument that the only real check on judges is the respect of peers, lawyers, and academics.
Chevron deference — the U.S. doctrine (1984-2024) that courts should defer to expert agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes; struck down in 2024.
Robert Plant, Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones, John 'Bonzo' Bonham — Led Zeppelin in full force on In Through the Out Door, just before Bonham's death and the band's break-up.
